path.title: BI, governance and performance
path.summary: Star schemas, history, semantic models, access control, lineage, and finding why a query is slow or wrong. Warehouse SQL and star checks run for real on the local catalog; lineage is static analysis; platform security rules are translated to DuckDB, not the vendors' engines.

lessons.title: Facts, dimensions and the star
lessons.summary: Declare the grain, keep dimensions wide and measures additive.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A fact table records events at one declared grain (one row per order line, per day and account...) with foreign keys and numeric measures. Dimensions describe the who, what, where and when in wide, denormalized tables joined directly to the fact: a star. Measures are additive (sales amount), semi-additive (a balance: sum across accounts, not across days) or non-additive (a ratio: recompute from its parts).

blocks.title: What this lab shows
blocks.body: The BI Lab runs warehouse SQL for real on the local DuckDB catalog and checks the star model (keys, grain, relationships) with real queries.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Mixing grains in one fact: an order-level shipping fee stored on every line is summed once per line.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: The example sums revenue per segment. Would the total change if dim_customer_segment had two rows for segment 1?

code.source:
SELECT s.segment_name,
       count(*)          AS orders,
       sum(o.net_amount) AS revenue
FROM source.orders AS o
JOIN source.dim_customer_segment AS s USING (segment_id)
GROUP BY s.segment_name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

visual.title: Facts, dimensions and the star - visual walkthrough

steps.title: The fact
steps.body: source.orders: one row per order, with a segment key and a measure.

steps.title: The dimension
steps.body: One row per segment: the join must not multiply orders.

steps.title: Aggregate
steps.body: Additive measures sum safely to the segment level.

steps.title: Check the grain
steps.body: Count rows before and after the join: they must match.

lessons.title: Keeping history: SCD types in practice
lessons.summary: Type 1 overwrites, type 2 versions, and facts join the version valid at the time.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Type 1 overwrites an attribute (corrections, or when history does not matter). Type 2 closes the current version (valid_to, is_current = false) and inserts a new one with a new surrogate key, so old facts keep pointing at the version that was true when they happened. Type 3 keeps only the previous value in an extra column. A point-in-time join matches the event date to the validity range.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Joining facts to a type 2 dimension on the business key alone: each fact matches every version and the totals multiply.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: C001 moved from Paris to Lyon on 15 September. Which city does an order of 10 September report, and which an order of 20 September?

code.source:
WITH dim_customer AS (
    SELECT * FROM (VALUES
        (1, 'C001', 'Paris', DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-09-15'),
        (2, 'C001', 'Lyon',  DATE '2026-09-15', DATE '9999-12-31')
    ) AS t(customer_sk, customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to)
),
sales AS (
    SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('C001', DATE '2026-09-10', 40.0), ('C001', DATE '2026-09-20', 60.0))
        AS t(customer_id, sale_date, amount)
)
SELECT s.sale_date, d.customer_sk, d.city, s.amount
FROM sales AS s
JOIN dim_customer AS d
  ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id
 AND s.sale_date >= d.valid_from AND s.sale_date < d.valid_to
ORDER BY s.sale_date;

visual.title: Keeping history: SCD types in practice - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Two versions
steps.body: Each version has its own surrogate key and a half-open validity range.

steps.title: Facts carry a date
steps.body: Each sale happened on one day.

steps.title: Point-in-time join
steps.body: Match the business key and the date inside [valid_from, valid_to).

steps.title: Result
steps.body: 10 September reports Paris, 20 September Lyon: history is preserved.

lessons.title: Semantic models and relationships
lessons.summary: Relationships, filter direction and storage modes in a Power BI-style model.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A semantic model sits between the tables and the reports: relationships (usually one-to-many from dimension to fact), measures, and how filters flow. With single cross-filter direction a slicer on a dimension filters the fact, not the other way round. A date dimension used for both order date and ship date is role-playing: one active relationship, the other inactive and activated in specific measures. Import mode stores a compressed copy refreshed on schedule; DirectQuery queries the source at report time; Direct Lake (Fabric) reads Delta tables in OneLake.

blocks.title: What this lab shows
blocks.body: The BI Lab star model file is Datapass's own format with Power BI's relationship vocabulary; there is no Power BI or DAX engine and no connection to one. Its checks (keys, cardinality, relationships) are real queries on the local catalog.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Setting every relationship to both directions to "make the visual work". It creates ambiguous filter paths and wrong totals that are hard to see.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Which relationship of the example must be inactive, and why can only one be active?

steps.title: Customer filters sales
steps.body: Many-to-one, single direction.

steps.title: Order date
steps.body: The active path from the date dimension.

steps.title: Ship date

steps.body: Filters flow from the one side to the many side.

lessons.title: Row, column and masking security
lessons.summary: Restrict rows by user, deny columns, mask what support agents see.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Row-level security attaches a predicate to a table so each principal reads only its rows (a rep sees their region). Column-level security grants or denies SELECT per column. Dynamic data masking changes what is shown to users without UNMASK; the stored values are unchanged, so it complements permissions rather than replacing them. Jobs run under their own service principal with only the grants they need.

blocks.title: What this lab shows
blocks.body: The Cloud Lab SQL pool tab enforces row-level security, column permissions and masking for real by rewriting each SELECT for its EXECUTE AS principal: T-SQL security translated to DuckDB, not SQL Server. The Databricks tab does the same for Unity Catalog row filters and column masks on SQL tasks.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Treating masking as encryption. A user who can filter WHERE salary > 100000 learns about masked values anyway.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: A rep runs SELECT SUM(amount) FROM sales. Does the total include other regions' rows?

visual.title: Row, column and masking security - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Predicate
steps.body: An inline function returns a row when the rep is the current user.

steps.title: Policy
steps.body: The security policy applies it as a filter on every read.

steps.title: Mask
steps.body: Email is shown masked to users without UNMASK.

steps.title: Aggregates too
steps.body: SUM and COUNT see only the filtered rows.

lessons.title: Lineage and personal data
lessons.summary: Follow a column downstream before you change it, and keep personal data where it belongs.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: Column lineage records which source columns each column is derived from. Read downstream for impact analysis (what breaks if I rename or redefine this column) and for privacy (which views expose an email address). Pseudonymised data, with names replaced by keys and the lookup kept apart, is still personal data under GDPR; only data that cannot reasonably be linked back to a person is anonymous.

blocks.title: What this lab shows
blocks.body: The BI Lab computes column lineage and impact as a static analysis of the SQL text with sqlglot: nothing is executed to obtain it. Unity Catalog and Microsoft Purview capture lineage from real runs on their platforms.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Hashing an email without a secret and calling it anonymous. Anyone with a list of emails can hash them and join.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: A shared view selects customer_key, city and a hash of email. Which of those columns trace back to personal data?

code.source:
WITH customers AS (
    SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('C001', 'ada@example.com', 'Paris'), ('C002', 'ben@example.com', 'Lyon'))
        AS t(customer_id, email, city)
)
SELECT md5(customer_id) AS customer_key,  -- derived from customer_id
       city                              -- copied from city
FROM customers;

visual.title: Lineage and personal data - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Sources
steps.body: customer_id and email identify a person; city does not on its own.

steps.title: Derived key
steps.body: customer_key derives from customer_id: an unsalted hash can be reversed by hashing known ids.

steps.title: Copied column
steps.body: city flows through unchanged.

steps.title: Not exposed
steps.body: email does not reach the view: the lineage shows no path.

lessons.title: Why is it slow, why is it wrong?
lessons.summary: Read the first error, check row counts at each join, prune files and partitions.

blocks.title: Wrong results
blocks.body: Most wrong totals come from a join that multiplies rows: a dimension with duplicate keys, a type 2 dimension joined on the business key, or a many-to-many without a bridge. Count rows before and after each join and check the key is unique on the one side.

blocks.title: Slow queries
blocks.body: Read the plan with real numbers (EXPLAIN ANALYZE in DuckDB or PostgreSQL, the Spark UI on a cluster). Look for scans that read every partition (no filter on the partition column), thousands of tiny files, one task far slower than the rest (skew), and SELECT * on wide tables. In logs, read the first failure and its innermost cause before the cascade that follows.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Fixing a duplicate total with SELECT DISTINCT. It hides the bad join and silently drops genuinely identical rows.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: The example adds a duplicate segment row on purpose. How many rows does the join return compared with the 12 orders?

code.source:
WITH segments AS (
    SELECT * FROM source.dim_customer_segment
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 1, 'Consumer (duplicate)'
)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM source.orders)           AS orders_before,
       count(*)                                      AS rows_after_join,
       sum(o.net_amount)                             AS revenue_after_join,
       (SELECT sum(net_amount) FROM source.orders)   AS true_revenue
FROM source.orders AS o
JOIN segments AS s USING (segment_id);

visual.title: Why is it slow, why is it wrong? - visual walkthrough

steps.title: Introduce a duplicate
steps.body: Segment 1 now has two rows.

steps.title: Count before
steps.body: The fact has 12 orders.

steps.title: Count after
steps.body: Every segment-1 order matches twice: more rows, inflated revenue.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: The true revenue differs; fix the key, not the symptom.
